public_rationale: The main point holds. Elluswamy, Tesla's Autopilot software director, testified that the 2016 video was meant to show what was possible to build, not what customers had. He also said the route was 3D-mapped in advance and that drivers had to take over during test runs. That supports 'staged' and 'aspirational, not real'. The more specific claim, 'not a single, unedited run', is contradicted by the same sworn testimony. Elluswamy said the published video was continuous and not stitched together, though it took several attempts to get a run with no interventions. Some secondary accounts say the video was edited, so that point is disputed, but the best primary source cuts against Marcus on it.
limitations: Elluswamy's statement about a single take is hedged ('my understanding').
Sped-up segments and camera cuts are a form of editing that the claim's wording may or may not cover.

our_interpretation: The claim has two parts. Part one: the 2016 'Paint It Black' video showed what Tesla hoped to build, not what the car could then do. Part two: the published footage was not one unedited run by one car.
Sworn testimony from people involved in making the video is the best evidence. News reports of that testimony count too.
'It seems' hedges the claim but does not empty it. Both parts are scored as factual assertions.
criteria.support_condition: Testimony or records show the video did not reflect real capability (pre-mapped route, failed attempts, features not available), and that the footage was spliced or edited from more than one run or car.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Testimony or records show the video was a real, representative capability demo, or that the published footage was one continuous, unstitched run.
